title: TLS, PKI, firewalls and VPNs
scopeHtml:
Scope: TLS handshake, certificates, mTLS, HSTS, firewalls, VPNs.

Scope: TLS handshake, certificates, mTLS, HSTS, firewalls, VPNs.

notes.title: What TLS gives you
notes.html:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) wraps a TCP connection so that nobody on the path can read or change the data, and you know who you are talking to. HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS. SSL is the dead ancestor; only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are acceptable today (1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated).

Three guarantees:

  • Confidentiality: data is encrypted (symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305).
  • Integrity: tampering is detected (AEAD authentication tags).
  • Authentication: the server proves its identity with a certificate (and optionally the client does too, mTLS).

Worked example. Symmetric encryption is fast (AES-NI: several GB/s per core), asymmetric (RSA, ECDSA) is slow (about 1,000 to 20,000 signatures/s per core). So TLS uses asymmetric crypto once, only to agree on a shared key, then symmetric for the data.

Industry examples. Let's Encrypt made free certificates routine (over 300M sites). Cloudflare, Google and Apple pushed TLS 1.3 and HTTPS-only (Chrome flags HTTP as "Not secure").

Everyday analogy. Two people use a public locker to exchange a secret code word, then talk in that code for the rest of the chat.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying TLS encrypts with the certificate's key. It uses a negotiated session key.
  • Thinking HTTPS hides the destination host entirely: the IP, and (without ECH) the SNI hostname, are visible.

notes.title: The TLS 1.3 handshake step by step
notes.html:
Goal: agree on keys and authenticate the server in as few round trips as possible. TLS 1.3 needs 1 RTT after TCP (TLS 1.2 needed 2).

Steps:

  1. ClientHello: supported versions, cipher suites, random, SNI (which hostname), ALPN (h2, http/1.1), and a key share (client's ephemeral Diffie-Hellman public value, X25519).
  2. ServerHello: picks cipher, sends its own key share. Both sides can now compute the shared secret; everything after is encrypted.
  3. EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify: the server sends its certificate chain and a signature over the transcript proving it holds the private key.
  4. Finished: both sides send a MAC over the handshake. Application data flows.
RTT = 40 ms (20 ms each way)
0 ms    SYN ------------------------->
40 ms   <------------------------- SYN-ACK        (TCP: 1 RTT)
40 ms   ClientHello (key share) ----->
80 ms   <---- ServerHello, Cert, Finished         (TLS: 1 RTT)
80 ms   Finished + GET / ------------>
100 ms  request reaches server; 120 ms first response byte arrives

So first byte after about 3 RTT = 120 ms from the start (TCP 1 + TLS 1 + request 1). TLS 1.2 would add one more RTT (160 ms).

Forward secrecy. The key share is ephemeral per connection (ECDHE). If the server's private key leaks later, old recorded traffic still cannot be decrypted. TLS 1.3 mandates it; static RSA key exchange was removed.

Session resumption and 0-RTT. After the first connection the server issues a ticket; the client resumes without the full certificate exchange. 0-RTT early data sends the request in the first flight, but it can be replayed by an attacker, so allow it only for idempotent requests.

Tool sample.

$ openssl s_client -connect api.shop.com:443 -servername api.shop.com -tls1_3
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Server certificate
subject=CN = api.shop.com
issuer=C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R3
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

Industry examples. TLS 1.3 handshakes cut mobile latency noticeably at Cloudflare and Facebook. HTTP/3 (QUIC) embeds this handshake into its own.

Decision gravity. Allowing old versions/ciphers for compatibility is reversible but a standing risk. Restrict to TLS 1.2+ with AEAD ciphers; verify partner/legacy clients first (check logs before turning off).

Everyday analogy. Meeting a stranger: you each whisper half of a secret across a crowded room such that only you two can combine it, then they show ID signed by an authority you trust.

Common interview traps.

  • Stating that TLS 1.2 and 1.3 have the same round trips.
  • Not mentioning ephemeral keys and forward secrecy.
  • Treating 0-RTT as safe for payments.

notes.title: Certificates and PKI
notes.html:
A certificate binds a public key to a name, signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) that clients already trust. PKI (public key infrastructure) is that whole trust system.

A certificate holds: subject and Subject Alternative Names (the hostnames that matter today, wildcard *.shop.com allowed), public key, validity dates (max 398 days for public TLS now, trending towards 90 days or less), issuer, key usage, and the issuer's signature.

Chain of trust. Leaf (your site) signed by an intermediate CA, signed by a root CA. Roots are shipped in the OS/browser trust store (about 150). Servers must send the leaf plus intermediates (not the root); a missing intermediate is a top cause of "works in Chrome, fails in curl or Android".

Validation by the client: chain signature verifies up to a trusted root; hostname matches a SAN; time within validity; not revoked; (Chrome) logged in Certificate Transparency.

Revocation. CRL (big list), OCSP (ask the CA per cert; slow and privacy-leaking), OCSP stapling (the server attaches a fresh signed response), and short-lived certificates (the modern answer: expire quickly, no revocation needed).

ACME and automation. Let's Encrypt issues certificates via the ACME protocol, proving control with an HTTP-01 file or DNS-01 TXT record (needed for wildcards). Renew at 60 days for a 90-day cert; cert-manager does this in Kubernetes.

Tool sample.

$ openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
subject=CN = api.shop.com
issuer=C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R3
notBefore=Oct  1 00:00:00 2026 GMT
notAfter=Dec 30 23:59:59 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:api.shop.com, DNS:www.shop.com

Real incident pattern. An expired certificate takes the service down on a fixed date and time. Examples: Microsoft Teams (2020), Spotify, Equifax's expired inspection cert hid their 2017 breach. Metric: days-to-expiry gauge alert at 30, 14, 7 days; synthetic probes using openssl s_client from outside.

Industry examples. Public CAs: DigiCert, Sectigo, Let's Encrypt, Google Trust Services. Private CAs: HashiCorp Vault PKI, AWS Private CA, Smallstep for internal services.

Decision gravity. Public vs private CA is hard to reverse for a fleet; automate issuance on day one. Certificate pinning in mobile apps raises security but can lock users out when you rotate (a one-way risk), so pin to a backup key or the CA, not the leaf.

Everyday analogy. A passport: your photo and name signed by a government that border guards trust, with an expiry date.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting the intermediate cert in the server chain.
  • CN-only certificates (hostnames come from SAN).
  • Manual renewals with no alerting.
  • Thinking a wildcard cert covers a.b.shop.com (it covers one label only).

notes.title: mTLS: both sides prove who they are
notes.html:
In mutual TLS the server also asks the client for a certificate, so both ends are authenticated cryptographically. The standard TLS flow gets a CertificateRequest from the server and a Certificate + CertificateVerify from the client.

Where it shines: service to service inside a company (zero trust), B2B APIs, device identity (IoT, Apple push), and Kubernetes service meshes.

  • Service mesh: Istio or Linkerd sidecars (Envoy) get short-lived certs (often 24 h) from the mesh CA, via SPIFFE identities like spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api, and rotate them automatically. App code is unchanged.
  • Authorization: the cert identity feeds policy ("only checkout may call payments").

Config (Istio).

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: { name: default, namespace: payments }
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

Worked example. 300 services with 24 h certs: each rotates daily, so ~300 certificate issuances/day, trivial for a CA; 1,500 pods x 12 renewals if cert life is 2 h. The cost is CA availability: if the mesh CA is down for longer than the cert lifetime, workloads lose identity.

Industry examples. Google ALTS, Lyft/Envoy, Uber and Netflix internal meshes, Cloudflare Access with client certs, and bank APIs (Open Banking) requiring mTLS.

Decision gravity. Starting with PERMISSIVE mode then moving to STRICT is the safe path (reversible). Retrofitting mTLS after a hundred services exist is far harder than starting with it.

Everyday analogy. Both the visitor and the building guard show badges, not just the guard.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking mTLS replaces user authentication. It identifies services/devices, not end users.
  • Long-lived client certs with no revocation story.
  • Debugging mTLS failures without knowing which side rejects (look for bad certificate, unknown ca alerts).

notes.title: HSTS and downgrade protection
notes.html:
HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) is a response header telling the browser "only ever use HTTPS for this site for the next N seconds". It stops SSL-stripping attacks where a man in the middle keeps a user on plain HTTP.

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload

  • Without it, the very first request to http://shop.com goes in clear text and is redirected; an attacker can intercept that moment.
  • Preload list: submit the domain to hstspreload.org, and browsers ship knowing it is HTTPS-only before ever visiting.
  • Related: secure cookies, upgrade-insecure-requests CSP, Certificate Transparency logs, CAA records (limit which CAs may issue), ECH (encrypted ClientHello hides SNI).

Rollout steps. Start with max-age=300, then 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 1 year. Verify every sub-domain serves valid HTTPS before adding includeSubDomains.

Decision gravity. Preload is practically a one-way door: removal takes months for browsers to ship, and a broken certificate becomes a hard failure (no click-through). Treat it as permanent.

Everyday analogy. A bank that tells you "never visit us except through the front door with guards" and puts it in your address book.

Common interview traps.

  • Enabling includeSubDomains with an old HTTP-only internal subdomain.
  • Sending the HSTS header over HTTP (ignored).
  • Believing HSTS stops phishing on lookalike domains; it does not.

notes.title: Firewalls
notes.html:
A firewall allows or denies traffic by rules on addresses, ports, protocols and (for smarter ones) application content.

Kinds:

  • Packet filter (stateless): each packet judged alone; fast, simple, cannot know about return traffic.
  • Stateful firewall: tracks connections (conntrack), so replies to allowed outbound connections are allowed automatically. Linux iptables/nftables, AWS Security Groups.
  • Network ACLs: stateless subnet-level rules (AWS NACL: you must allow return ports).
  • Application layer / WAF: inspects HTTP (SQL injection, XSS, bots); AWS WAF, Cloudflare WAF, ModSecurity.
  • Next-gen firewalls: deep packet inspection, TLS inspection, identity-aware rules.

Principles: default deny, least privilege, allow by security group reference rather than IP, log drops.

Config (Linux nftables).

nft add table inet filter
nft add chain inet filter input '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }'
nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept
nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport { 22, 443 } accept
nft add rule inet filter input iif lo accept

Worked example (three tier). ALB SG: allow 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. App SG: allow 8080 only from the ALB SG. DB SG: allow 5432 only from the App SG. A compromised web page cannot talk to the DB directly even though they share a VPC.

Real incident pattern. "Connection timed out" (packets silently dropped by a firewall) versus "connection refused" (host replied RST: reachable but nothing listening). Timeouts usually mean a firewall or routing issue. Conntrack table full (nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet in dmesg) on busy NAT/boxes: size it with net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max.

Industry examples. AWS Security Groups and NACLs, GCP VPC firewall, Palo Alto and Fortinet appliances, Cloudflare Magic Firewall.

Decision gravity. Wide-open rules (0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 or the DB) are easy to add, hard to audit later. Prefer SSM/bastion/Zero Trust access over open SSH.

Everyday analogy. A building's reception with a guest list (rules) and a log of who came in and left.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing stateless NACLs with stateful security groups.
  • Exposing databases to the internet "temporarily".
  • Thinking a firewall alone secures an app; WAF and auth still matter.

notes.title: VPNs
notes.html:
A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device or network and another network, so traffic travels privately over the public internet.

Types:

  • Remote access VPN: laptop to company network (OpenVPN, WireGuard, IPsec/IKEv2, Cisco AnyConnect).
  • Site-to-site VPN: office or datacentre to a cloud VPC (AWS Site-to-Site VPN, two IPsec tunnels for redundancy).
  • Mesh / overlay VPN: WireGuard-based Tailscale or ZeroTier connects devices peer to peer.
  • Split vs full tunnel: split sends only corporate ranges through the tunnel; full sends everything.

Protocols: IPsec (kernel, standard in enterprises; IKE negotiates keys; ESP encrypts), OpenVPN (TLS-based, user space, flexible), WireGuard (about 4,000 lines of code, modern cryptography, fast, in the Linux kernel since 5.6).

Config (WireGuard).

# /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf  (INI format)
# [Interface]
# PrivateKey = <laptop key>
# Address = 10.8.0.2/32
# [Peer]
# PublicKey = <gateway key>
# Endpoint = vpn.shop.com:51820
# AllowedIPs = 10.0.0.0/16        # split tunnel: only the VPC range
# PersistentKeepalive = 25

Worked example. Tunnels add headers (WireGuard ~60 to 80 bytes), reducing the effective MTU from 1500 to about 1420. Ignoring this causes the mysterious "small requests work, large ones hang" bug (see debugging notes: set MSS clamping or MTU).

Industry examples. Tailscale, Cloudflare WARP, Google BeyondCorp (zero trust that replaces broad VPN access with per-app identity-aware proxies), AWS Client VPN.

Decision gravity. A broad VPN gives network-level access once in (lateral movement risk). Zero-trust/identity-aware access is the direction, but it is a larger migration. Site-to-site links are reversible but need non-overlapping CIDR ranges chosen up front (overlap is a painful one-way mistake).

Everyday analogy. A sealed armoured truck driving over public roads between two private warehouses.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a VPN makes you anonymous; the VPN provider sees your traffic.
  • Overlapping CIDR blocks between networks.
  • Forgetting MTU/MSS issues and DNS routing (split DNS) in tunnels.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• TLS = confidentiality, integrity, authentication; asymmetric crypto only to agree on a key, then fast symmetric encryption.
  • TLS 1.3 handshake: ClientHello with key share, ServerHello + cert + Finished, then data: 1 RTT; ephemeral keys give forward secrecy; 0-RTT is replayable.
  • Certificates bind keys to names via SAN, chain leaf to intermediate to root; send intermediates; automate renewal (ACME) and alert on expiry.
  • mTLS authenticates both ends; meshes (Istio, Linkerd) automate short-lived certs with STRICT mode.
  • HSTS forces HTTPS; roll out slowly; preload is near-permanent.
  • Firewalls: default deny, stateful vs stateless, security groups by reference, WAF for L7; timeout = dropped, refused = RST.
  • VPNs tunnel traffic (IPsec, OpenVPN, WireGuard); mind split tunnel, CIDR overlap and MTU.

questions.promptHtml: What does TLS give you, and why does it use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A basic check that you can separate confidentiality, integrity and authentication, and know where the certificate's key is (and is not) used.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TLS gives confidentiality (data is encrypted), integrity (tampering is detected) and authentication (the server proves identity with a certificate, optionally the client too). Asymmetric crypto is slow, around thousands of signatures per second per core, so TLS uses it once to agree on a shared key and authenticate, then switches to fast symmetric encryption like AES-GCM, several GB/s per core with AES-NI.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App (HTTP) -> TLS -> TCP -> IP
Handshake : asymmetric (ECDHE key agreement + certificate signature)  -> session keys
Data      : symmetric AEAD (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305) with those keys

The certificate's key does not encrypt the traffic. It signs the handshake transcript to prove identity; the traffic key comes from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman. AEAD gives encryption and an authentication tag in one operation. Only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are acceptable today. What TLS does not hide: the destination IP, packet sizes and timing, and (without ECH) the SNI hostname.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "TLS encrypts with the server certificate's public key": it uses a negotiated session key.
  • "HTTPS hides which site I visit": IP and SNI remain visible.
  • Confusing TLS authentication with user authentication.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is AES-GCM faster than RSA? -> Block cipher with hardware instructions versus big-number math.
  2. What is AEAD? -> Authenticated encryption with associated data: one pass gives secrecy and tamper detection.
  3. What does ECH change? -> Encrypts the ClientHello (including SNI) so observers cannot see the hostname.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE recites "encryption and certificates". Senior separates the three guarantees, says what leaks (IP, SNI, size), and explains that the cert signs, the ephemeral key encrypts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team assumed TLS to a partner hid hostnames from the corporate firewall; the firewall still filtered on SNI, and an ECH rollout later broke that policy.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake and tell me how many round trips it adds to a new HTTPS request.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Latency reasoning: candidates who can count RTTs can reason about CDN placement, connection reuse and HTTP/3.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: After the TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 needs one round trip. The client sends ClientHello with its ephemeral key share; the server answers ServerHello with its key share, then certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished, all encrypted; the client sends Finished plus the HTTP request. TLS 1.2 needed two round trips, so TLS 1.3 saves one RTT.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RTT = 40 ms
0 ms    SYN ------------------------->
40 ms   <------------------------- SYN-ACK         (TCP: 1 RTT)
40 ms   ClientHello (SNI, ALPN, key share) ---->
80 ms   <---- ServerHello, Cert, CertVerify, Finished   (TLS: 1 RTT)
80 ms   Finished + GET / ------------>
120 ms  first response byte arrives (3 RTT total incl. request)

ClientHello carries versions, ciphers, random, SNI, ALPN (h2) and the X25519 key share. Both sides derive the shared secret after ServerHello, so everything after is encrypted. Resumption tickets skip the certificate exchange; 0-RTT early data sends the request in the first flight.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
$ openssl s_client -connect api.shop.com:443 -servername api.shop.com -tls1_3 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'New,|Verify return'
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying TLS 1.2 and 1.3 have the same round trips.
  • Forgetting the TCP RTT before TLS.
  • Treating 0-RTT as safe for non-idempotent requests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does QUIC change it? -> It merges transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes: 1 RTT for new, 0 RTT for resumed.
  2. Why does SNI go in the ClientHello? -> Server needs the hostname to pick the right certificate before it can reply.
  3. What does ALPN do? -> Negotiates h2 vs http/1.1 inside the handshake, no extra RTT.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists messages. Senior counts RTTs against real distance (Mumbai to Frankfurt ~120 ms RTT so 3 RTT = 360 ms), and proposes connection reuse, edge termination, or resumption.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Moving TLS termination to an edge POS near users cut first-byte time for cold mobile sessions by roughly the distance saved times 2 RTT.

questions.promptHtml: How does a client decide to trust a server's certificate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Certificate failures are a top outage cause; the signal is knowing each check and which one usually fails.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The client builds a chain from the server's leaf certificate through intermediates to a root already in its trust store, verifying each signature. It also checks that the hostname matches a Subject Alternative Name, the dates are valid, the certificate is not revoked, and (Chrome) that it appears in Certificate Transparency logs. The server must send the leaf and intermediates, not the root.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Root CA (in trust store, ~150) -> Intermediate CA -> Leaf (api.shop.com)

Leaf fields: SAN list (hostnames live here, CN is legacy), public key, notBefore/notAfter (public max 398 days, trending lower), issuer, key usage. A wildcard *.shop.com covers exactly one label: a.shop.com yes, a.b.shop.com no. Revocation: CRL, OCSP, OCSP stapling, or short-lived certs. Automation: ACME (Let's Encrypt) via HTTP-01 or DNS-01 (needed for wildcards), renew at 60 days of 90.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
$ openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
subject=CN = api.shop.com
issuer=C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R3
notAfter=Dec 30 23:59:59 2026 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:api.shop.com, DNS:www.shop.com

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to send the intermediate: works in Chrome (which can fetch it), fails in curl, Java and Android.
  • Matching hostnames against CN only.
  • No expiry alerting.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is OCSP stapling better than plain OCSP? -> No client call to the CA (privacy, latency); the server attaches a fresh signed response.
  2. What is Certificate Transparency? -> Public append-only logs of issued certs so misissuance is detectable.
  3. What is a CAA record? -> DNS record restricting which CAs may issue for the domain.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "CA signs it". Senior lists every check, knows the missing-intermediate trap, and automates issuance with ACME and expiry alerts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Certificate expiries are fixed-time outages that have taken down very large products; a days-to-expiry gauge alerting at 30/14/7 days prevents them.

questions.promptHtml: What is forward secrecy, and why is TLS 1.3 0-RTT dangerous?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand why ephemeral keys exist and the replay trade-off behind a latency feature.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Forward secrecy means each connection uses an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key, so if the server's long-term private key leaks later, previously recorded traffic still cannot be decrypted. TLS 1.3 mandates it. 0-RTT lets a resuming client send data in its first flight using the previous session's secret, but an attacker can replay that first flight, so I only allow it for idempotent requests.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
With static RSA key exchange (TLS 1.2 option), the client encrypted the premaster secret to the server's cert key: anyone who records traffic and later steals the key decrypts everything. With ECDHE each side generates a throwaway key pair per connection and discards it. Session secrets are derived from the DH output.

0-RTT: the early data is encrypted with a key derived from the resumption secret, so there is no fresh server contribution, hence no replay protection at the TLS layer. Mitigations: servers accept 0-RTT only on safe methods (GET), keep single-use ticket stores (hard in a cluster), or reject early data (425 Too Early).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking session tickets (TLS 1.2) provide forward secrecy: a long-lived ticket key breaks it.
  • Allowing 0-RTT on POST /pay.
  • Calling HTTPS "unbreakable" without mentioning endpoint compromise.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does a replay matter? -> A replayed POST /transfer executes twice.
  2. How does a CDN handle it? -> Forwards early data with an Early-Data: 1 header; origin returns 425 for unsafe requests.
  3. Is rotating the ticket key relevant? -> Yes, rotate often (hours) to bound exposure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines forward secrecy. Senior contrasts static RSA vs ECDHE, ties ticket key rotation to FS, and states the idempotency rule for 0-RTT.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A CDN enabling 0-RTT without telling the origin led to duplicate form submissions on flaky mobile networks; the origin had to honor Early-Data.

questions.contextHtml:
After renewing a certificate, the mobile team reports "SSL handshake failed" on Android 9 and the partner's Java batch job throws PKIX path building failed. Chrome and Safari on laptops are fine. Monitoring (an HTTP check from a Chrome-based probe) is green. You run:

$ openssl s_client -connect api.shop.com:443 -servername api.shop.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -E 's:|i:|Verify'
 0 s:CN = api.shop.com
   i:C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R3
Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)

Only one certificate is shown in the chain. Expiry is Jan 2027. The ops engineer says "the cert is valid, the clients are broken".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and explain why Chrome works.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Update the Android trust store" or "disable verification". Misses that the server omitted the intermediate.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the renewal (new cert file, different bundle)? Which clients fail (non-browser)? Is TLS terminated on an LB or the app?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Install the full chain (leaf + intermediate) on the terminator and reload; no client change.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: incomplete chain sent; wrong intermediate for the issuing CA; expired intermediate; client trust store missing the new root.
  4. How I'd verify each: openssl s_client -showcerts counting certs; openssl verify -untrusted inter.pem leaf.pem; check issuer of leaf equals subject of intermediate; compare with curl -v https://api.shop.com on a clean Linux box.
  5. Root cause: the server sent only the leaf. Browsers cache or fetch missing intermediates via the AIA extension, so they succeeded; curl, Java and older Android do not fetch, so they cannot build the path.
  6. Fix: configure ssl_certificate with fullchain.pem (leaf then intermediates, never the root):
# nginx
ssl_certificate     /etc/ssl/api.shop.com/fullchain.pem;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/api.shop.com/privkey.pem;

Long term: renewal tooling that always writes the fullchain. 7. Prevention: synthetic probe with openssl s_client and curl from a minimal container (not a browser) that fails on verify code != 0; days-to-expiry alert. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not telling partners to disable verification (-k/trust all); not pinning a leaf to hide the problem.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Chain is complete but Android 7 still fails? -> Old devices lack the new root (ISRG Root X1 cross-sign issue); use a chain with a cross-signed root for compatibility.
  • Cert is for api.shop.com but clients use api2.shop.com? -> SAN mismatch; verify with -ext subjectAltName.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A renewal passed every browser test and broke a partner's nightly Java job at 2 a.m. The fix was one file name (cert.pem to fullchain.pem) and a non-browser probe.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames clients or disables verification.
  • Hire: spots the missing intermediate with openssl and fixes the chain.
  • Strong hire: explains AIA fetching, adds non-browser probes, mentions old-root compatibility.

questions.contextHtml:
At 03:14 on a Sunday, every call to the internal billing API failed with x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid: current time 2026-10-18T03:14:02Z is after 2026-10-18T03:00:00Z. Time to detect: 41 minutes (a customer ticket). Time to fix: 2 h 10 min because only one engineer knew where the cert lived. Facts from the review:

$ openssl x509 -in /etc/billing/tls.crt -noout -enddate
notAfter=Oct 18 03:00:00 2026 GMT
cert-manager Certificate status: "Issuing... Order failed: DNS-01 challenge TXT record not found"
last successful renewal: Jul 20 2026 (90 day cert)

cert-manager logs had warned for 25 days. Nobody was subscribed to them. An exemption existed because the DNS API token was rotated in September.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review: causes, actions, and how you would make this class of outage impossible.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Renew earlier" or "set a calendar reminder". Treats it as a human reminder problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns issuance? Are there other certs on the same issuer and token? What is the full inventory of certs and expiries? Which alert should have fired?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the DNS-01 credential, force reissue (cmctl renew), reload pods; as fallback issue a manual cert.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: broken ACME auth after token rotation (confirmed by order error); alerting gap; ownership gap; single point of failure in DNS provider credential.
  4. How I'd verify each: kubectl describe certificate/order/challenge; Prometheus certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds; scan fleet with openssl s_client for all endpoints.
  5. Root cause: token rotation was not propagated to cert-manager, so renewals silently failed for 25 days; no alert tied to remaining validity; no owner.
  6. Fix: corrective actions: fleet-wide expiry gauge with alerts at 30/14/7/3 days to on-call; test credentials in the rotation runbook; synthetic external probe; renew at 2/3 lifetime so failures have 30 days of buffer; shorter certs only once alerting exists.
  7. Prevention: inventory via CT logs and scanning; blameless review with action owners and dates; game-day that revokes the DNS token.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not blaming the engineer; not lengthening cert lifetime to avoid renewals (raises risk, and public max is 398 days anyway).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• CA rate limits hit during the retry storm? -> Back off; use staging endpoint for tests; keep an alternate CA configured.
  • 90-day to 47-day lifetimes coming? -> Automation is mandatory; manual renewal does not scale (verify current CA/B Forum schedule).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments org had 19 expiries in a year until a single dashboard tracked every endpoint's days-to-expiry; the number of expiry incidents went to zero without changing any cert lifetime.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "set reminders".
  • Hire: traces to failed ACME auth and adds metric-based alerting.
  • Strong hire: ownership, inventory, credential rotation tests, renewal buffer and game-day.

questions.contextHtml:
A new private subnet for a reporting service connects to an RDS Postgres (10.1.5.20:5432). The SG on RDS allows 5432 from the reporting SG. The team also added a custom NACL on the DB subnet:

Inbound  rule 100  ALLOW tcp 5432      from 10.1.8.0/24
Inbound  rule *    DENY  all
Outbound rule 100  ALLOW tcp 5432      to   10.1.8.0/24
Outbound rule *    DENY  all

From a reporting host:

$ nc -zv -w 5 10.1.5.20 5432
nc: connect to 10.1.5.20 port 5432 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress
$ sudo tcpdump -nn -i any host 10.1.5.20
10:02:11.1 IP 10.1.8.14.51234 > 10.1.5.20.5432: Flags [S]
10:02:12.1 IP 10.1.8.14.51234 > 10.1.5.20.5432: Flags [S]
10:02:14.1 IP 10.1.8.14.51234 > 10.1.5.20.5432: Flags [S]

The SGs have been checked three times and look right.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and why does SG-only checking miss it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Rechecks the SG for the fourth time. Does not know NACLs are stateless.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a NACL on both subnets? Is route table correct? Do SYN retries show a SYN-ACK anywhere? Was this working before the NACL?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the missing return-traffic rule or revert to the default allow-all NACL temporarily.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: stateless NACL blocking return traffic; NACL on the reporting subnet blocking the outbound ephemeral port; route table missing; RDS SG source mismatch.
  4. How I'd verify each: VPC Flow Logs: ACCEPT on inbound request, REJECT on the reply; Reachability Analyzer; tcpdump on a host in the DB subnet showing SYN-ACK leaving.
  5. Root cause: security groups are stateful; NACLs are stateless. The DB subnet NACL allows inbound 5432 but its outbound rule only allows destination port 5432, while the reply goes to the client's ephemeral port (1024-65535). The SYN-ACK is dropped, so the client sees SYN retries at 1, 2, 4 s and a timeout.
  6. Fix: outbound ALLOW tcp 1024-65535 to 10.1.8.0/24 on the DB subnet; the reporting subnet needs the mirror: outbound 5432 and inbound 1024-65535 from the DB subnet.
  7. Prevention: avoid custom NACLs unless needed; manage via IaC with a test (nc -zv from a probe); Flow Logs enabled.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not opening 0.0.0.0/0 all on the NACL; that discards the layer. Not widening the SG.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same symptom but a connection refused? -> Reached the host, nothing listening (RST); not a firewall drop.
  • Why SYN retries at 1, 2, 4 s? -> Initial RTO 1 s with exponential backoff.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration stalled for a day because three people re-verified SGs; a Flow Logs query showed REJECT on return packets in two minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps editing SGs.
  • Hire: identifies stateless NACL ephemeral port issue.
  • Strong hire: uses Flow Logs/tcpdump evidence, writes both-direction rules, prefers SG-only design.

questions.promptHtml: What does HSTS protect against, and how would you roll it out safely?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: HSTS has a one-way door (preload); the signal is whether you stage it and know what it does not cover.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HSTS is a response header that tells the browser to use HTTPS only for this host for the next max-age seconds, which defeats SSL-stripping on the first plain-HTTP hop. I roll it out gradually: max-age 300, then a day, a week, a month, a year; add includeSubDomains only after every subdomain serves valid HTTPS; consider preload last because it is nearly permanent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload

Without it, the first request to http://shop.com is plaintext and gets a 301; a man in the middle can intercept that and keep the user on HTTP. After HSTS, the browser rewrites http:// to https:// internally and refuses click-through on certificate errors. The header is ignored over plain HTTP. Preload bakes the domain into browsers, protecting even the first visit, but removal takes months to propagate. Complementary controls: Secure cookies, CAA records, Certificate Transparency monitoring, ECH.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• includeSubDomains while an old internal subdomain only speaks HTTP.
  • Believing HSTS stops phishing on lookalike domains.
  • Preloading before certificate automation is solid: a broken cert becomes a hard failure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not send HSTS on HTTP? -> Attacker could inject it; browsers ignore it over plain HTTP.
  2. How do you undo it? -> Serve max-age=0 over HTTPS; users only clear it when they revisit; preload removal is slow.
  3. Does it help API clients like curl? -> No, it is a browser feature.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "forces HTTPS". Senior stages max-age, audits subdomains first, and treats preload as irreversible.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A company with a forgotten legacy.shop.com HTTP-only host enabled includeSubDomains and broke an internal tool for every Chrome user.

questions.contextHtml:
You are connecting the company's 10.0.0.0/16 on-prem network to an AWS VPC and to an acquired company's network, via two IPsec tunnels each. The VPC was created with the default 10.0.0.0/16. The acquired company uses 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.1.0.0/16. Users report that after a prototype link, internal DNS names resolve but pings go to the wrong machines:

$ ip route get 10.0.4.22
10.0.4.22 dev eth0 src 10.0.1.5
$ ping 10.0.4.22
64 bytes from 10.0.4.22: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.4 ms   # answered by a LOCAL host

The team wants to use NAT between networks to avoid renumbering. Throughput needed: 800 Mbit/s, one tunnel ~1.25 Gbit/s max.
questions.promptHtml: What is your plan, and what would you avoid?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a static route"; ignores the longest-prefix-match issue with identical CIDRs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can any network be renumbered? How many hosts need cross-connectivity? Is traffic initiated both ways? Is a transit gateway in use? Is DNS split?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not connect overlapping ranges; keep the prototype isolated to avoid misdirected traffic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: identical CIDRs make the local route win; static routes cannot disambiguate; NAT adds state and breaks protocols embedding IPs.
  4. How I'd verify each: ip route get, route tables of VPC/TGW, traceroute -n showing the first hop stays local; compare ARP replies.
  5. Root cause: a router picks the most specific prefix; with the same /16 on both sides, the local connected route always wins, so remote hosts are unreachable and local ones answer instead.
  6. Fix: renumber the VPC to a unique range (for example 10.20.0.0/16) while it is still young; for the acquired network use 1:1 NAT or a NAT-ed shared service subnet only for the few services needed. Pick two tunnels on separate endpoints; verify 800 Mbit/s fits one tunnel with headroom or use ECMP across both (TGW).
  7. Prevention: a central IPAM with allocated ranges and a policy (never use 10.0.0.0/16 default); MTU for IPsec ~1400 plus MSS clamp.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not NAT-everything as the permanent design: debugging, logs and ACLs become ambiguous. Renumbering is painful but cheapest early; overlap is a one-way mistake.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cannot renumber the acquired side? -> NAT the foreign side into an unused /24 for the specific services and document it.
  • DNS returns the real IP, not the NAT-ed one? -> Needs DNS rewriting or a private zone with NAT-ed addresses.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A merger inherited 10.0.0.0/16 on both sides. The 3-month renumbering looked costly; the alternative of permanent NAT was still burning on-call hours years later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds static routes.
  • Hire: explains longest-prefix match and plans renumbering or limited NAT.
  • Strong hire: IPAM governance, MTU/MSS, ECMP/capacity and DNS handling.

questions.promptHtml: How does mTLS work in a service mesh, what does it actually prove, and what are its failure modes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Zero-trust is common; the signal is knowing it authenticates workloads, not users, and that it has an operational dependency (the CA).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: In mTLS the server sends a CertificateRequest and the client presents its own certificate plus a CertificateVerify, so both sides are authenticated. In a mesh, each sidecar gets a short-lived certificate from the mesh CA carrying a SPIFFE identity such as spiffe://prod/ns/payments/sa/api, rotates it automatically, and an authorization policy says which identities may call which service. It proves which workload is calling, not which user; and if the CA is down longer than the cert lifetime, workloads lose identity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Service A -> Sidecar A --(mTLS, cert SAN: spiffe://prod/ns/checkout/sa/web)--> Sidecar B -> Service B
Policy: allow principal checkout/web to call payments/api POST /charge

Cert lifetime is a trade: 24 h certs means a daily rotation with a bounded revocation window; 2 h certs shrink exposure but make the CA a hotter dependency (1,500 pods x 12 renewals/day). The sidecar keeps working with the old cert until expiry, so a CA outage only bites after the lifetime passes. Debugging alerts: bad certificate (a side rejected the peer), unknown ca (missing root), certificate expired. PERMISSIVE mode accepts plaintext and mTLS; STRICT demands mTLS.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata: { name: default, namespace: payments }
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating mTLS as end-user authentication.
  • Long-lived client certs with no revocation or rotation story.
  • Debugging without knowing which side rejected.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the mesh CA is down? -> Existing certs work until expiry; alert at 50% of lifetime without renewal.
  2. How is identity enforced? -> AuthorizationPolicy on SPIFFE principal, namespace, service account.
  3. Cost? -> Sidecar CPU and latency (low ms), cert management; ambient/ztunnel designs reduce it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "both sides have certs". Senior adds SPIFFE identities, short lifetimes, authorization policy, CA dependency and rollout modes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mesh root CA expired after a 1-year default; every workload lost trust at once. Root and intermediate rotation became a rehearsed runbook.

questions.contextHtml:
You must turn on mesh-wide mTLS STRICT for 180 services (about 40k rps total) in 6 weeks for a compliance audit, with no customer-visible errors. Today the mesh is in PERMISSIVE. Telemetry after enabling STRICT in one pilot namespace (payments) for 5 minutes:

istio_requests_total{response_code="0", response_flags="UC", destination_service="payments-api"}   +2,140
envoy log: upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection termination
curl from legacy-batch (no sidecar) -> payments-api:8080: curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer
kube-probe liveness for payments-api: Get "http://10.4.2.9:8080/health": connection reset by peer

The pilot was rolled back after pod restarts began.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how do you complete the rollout safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Flip STRICT mesh-wide on the weekend". Ignores non-mesh clients and probes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which callers lack sidecars (batch jobs, cron, other clusters, ingress)? How are health probes done? Any headless/StatefulSet services with their own TLS? Are there external clients?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the namespace back to PERMISSIVE (already done); add portLevelMtls exceptions only where needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: non-mesh clients sending plaintext; kubelet probes sent plaintext and rejected under STRICT; sidecar not injected on some pods; clients with hard-coded http:// to pod IPs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Istio telemetry for connection_security_policy=none by source; istioctl x describe pod; istioctl proxy-status; compare liveness probe config (Istio rewrites probes with sidecar.istio.io/rewriteAppHTTPProbers).
  5. Root cause: STRICT rejects any plaintext. Legacy batch had no sidecar, and the probe rewrite was disabled on that deployment, so kubelet's plaintext probes got RST; failing liveness restarted pods.
  6. Fix (plan): week 1-2 inventory plaintext callers using PERMISSIVE telemetry; week 2-4 onboard clients (inject sidecars, or egress gateway with mTLS); fix probes; week 4-5 enable STRICT namespace by namespace with a 24 h soak and error-budget gate; week 6 mesh-wide default plus a policy forbidding new PERMISSIVE.
  7. Prevention: admission policy requiring injection; dashboard of plaintext traffic by source; audit evidence via PeerAuthentication in Git.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not mesh-wide flip. Not leaving permanent exceptions without an expiry date.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Third-party SaaS agents can't join the mesh? -> Terminate mTLS at an ingress gateway with its own authenticated front door.
  • Auditor wants the evidence? -> Metrics showing 100% mutual_tls connection_security_policy and the config in Git.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A big-bang STRICT flip restarted 400 pods when probes were rejected. The retry was namespace-by-namespace with plaintext-source telemetry, and finished two weeks later without an incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: global flip.
  • Hire: staged by namespace with PERMISSIVE telemetry, handles probes and non-mesh clients.
  • Strong hire: error-budget gates, exception expiry, audit evidence.

questions.contextHtml:
Security enabled Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload on the apex shop.com and submitted it to the preload list on Monday. Thursday, support gets reports that status.shop.com and ops.shop.com are unreachable for many Chrome and Firefox users. Edge/Safari mobile users on older versions are fine.

$ curl -sI https://status.shop.com
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name 'status.shop.com'
$ curl -sI http://ops.shop.com
HTTP/1.1 200 OK        # plain HTTP only, port 443 closed
browser: NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID  (no "Proceed anyway" button)

status.shop.com is a third-party hosted page with a cert for shop.statuspage.example. ops.shop.com is an internal tool served over HTTP.
questions.promptHtml: What happened, how do you restore service, and what do you tell leadership?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove the header" or "wait it out". Does not know the preload list and cached HSTS cannot be turned off quickly.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which subdomains exist (DNS zone audit)? Who owns each? Can each get valid HTTPS fast? Is the domain already in the browser preload list yet?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put valid HTTPS in front of each affected host: ACME cert for ops.shop.com at a reverse proxy; for status get the vendor's custom-domain TLS or CNAME to a provider that supports it; or temporarily point the name to a redirect page.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: includeSubDomains applied to HTTP-only or mismatched-cert hosts; preload already shipped in browsers; cached HSTS in users' browsers from the header.
  4. How I'd verify each: export the DNS zone and list all records; probe each host with curl -sI https://host and openssl s_client -servername host; check hstspreload.org status.
  5. Root cause: includeSubDomains made browsers force HTTPS on every subdomain with no certificate-error override. Subdomains with no HTTPS or a wrong certificate became hard failures. The header was cached (up to 2 years) and preload submission makes it nearly permanent.
  6. Fix: short-term: provide valid TLS on each subdomain. Long-term: subdomain inventory in IaC with an HTTPS check gate; remove from the preload list via hstspreload.org (takes months to roll out in browsers); lower max-age to 0 over HTTPS where served so cached entries expire for returning visitors.
  7. Prevention: staged rollout (300 s -> 1 year), per-subdomain HTTPS audit before includeSubDomains, preload only after one-year clean operation; synthetic checks on all hostnames.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not serving a self-signed cert (users cannot proceed anyway); not disabling HSTS on the apex as the only action since preload persists.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cannot get valid TLS for the vendor-hosted page? -> Move to a different parent domain (status.shop-status.example) and update links.
  • Executive asks to "just roll it back"? -> Explain rollback is months for preload; the fast path is making the sites valid HTTPS.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-meant preload submission broke a forgotten admin subdomain for a quarter. Afterward the company required a zone-wide HTTPS audit and a 4-week staged max-age schedule for any header change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries to remove the header and expects immediate effect.
  • Hire: understands includeSubDomains and the cache/preload permanence, fixes TLS on subdomains.
  • Strong hire: inventory gate, staged rollout policy, communication plan.

questions.contextHtml:
A Linux NAT/egress gateway VM (8 vCPU, 16 GB) for 400 app servers starts dropping new connections at peak (18k new conns/s). Existing connections work. Intermittent client symptom: connect timeout. Gateway evidence:

$ dmesg -T | tail -3
[Tue Nov 10 14:02:11] nf_conntrack: nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet
$ sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 262144
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count = 262144
$ conntrack -S | head -2
cpu=0 found=1830 invalid=9 insert_failed=41022 drop=41022 early_drop=0 ...
$ sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_time_wait = 120
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established = 432000

CPU 35%, bandwidth 1.2 Gbit/s of 10. Red herring: a recent change added a UDP DNS rule.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add CPU" or "restart the box". Does not see the conntrack table as the limiting resource.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the connection churn rate and typical lifetime? Are many connections idle (long-lived)? Is conntrack on a node with stateful rules or could it be skipped? Any DNS query storm?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise nf_conntrack_max (memory permitting: roughly 300 bytes per entry) and adjust the hash size; reduce tcp_timeout_established from 5 days.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: table full from long established timeout; TIME_WAIT entries kept 120 s; UDP DNS entries (30 s) in huge volume; a connection leak by one client.
  4. How I'd verify each: conntrack -L | awk '{print $4}' | sort | uniq -c by state; conntrack -L -p udp | wc -l; conntrack -L | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head for top source IPs.
  5. Root cause: count equals max (262,144), so new flows are dropped (insert_failed/drop). 18k new conns/s x 120 s TIME_WAIT = 2.1M possible entries, and established idle flows are retained for 5 days. The table is the bottleneck, not CPU or bandwidth.
  6. Fix: short-term: sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=2097152, nf_conntrack_buckets=524288, tcp_timeout_established=3600, tcp_timeout_time_wait=30. Long-term: apps use connection pooling and keep-alive to cut churn; spread egress over several NAT gateways; exempt flows that need no state with NOTRACK in the raw table; monitor nf_conntrack_count / max.
  7. Prevention: alert at 70% of table; per-source limits; load test at 2x.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not setting max huge without sizing RAM; not shortening established timeout below app keepalives (kills idle DB connections: use TCP keepalive at 60 s or less).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same issue in Kubernetes nodes? -> kube-proxy and CNI use conntrack; DNS-heavy pods fill it; NodeLocal DNSCache helps.
  • Why was the DNS rule a red herring? -> UDP entries expire in 30 s; counts by protocol show TCP dominates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A NAT VM looked healthy on every dashboard except a log line. Tuning the established timeout from 5 days to 1 hour dropped the table from full to 18% with no hardware change.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or scales CPU.
  • Hire: identifies conntrack exhaustion and raises limits.
  • Strong hire: quantifies entries, tunes timeouts, reduces churn, adds alerting and NOTRACK where valid.

questions.contextHtml:
An API edge terminates TLS on 6 nodes (16 vCPU each) and sees 12k new connections/s at peak, using about 55% CPU. A campaign expects 10x. Perf output on one node:

perf top: 31% libcrypto: rsaz_2048_sqr / ossl_ecp_nistz256_*
openssl speed rsa2048: sign 1,450/s per core
Session reuse ratio (ssl_session_reused): 12%
Most traffic: mobile apps opening a new connection per request over 4G (RTT 80 ms)

Certificate: RSA 2048. HTTP/1.1 with Connection: close on 40% of client libraries.
questions.promptHtml: How do you survive 10x handshakes without 10x servers?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add 60 nodes". Never reduces handshake cost or frequency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can we change the client libs? Do we have a CDN/edge? Is the key exportable to an HSM? What share is resumed already?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pre-scale 2x and enable session tickets/caching so repeat clients skip full handshakes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: full handshakes dominate; RSA signing is the CPU hog; low reuse ratio; clients closing connections.
  4. How I'd verify each: openssl speed rsa2048 ecdsap256; nginx $ssl_session_reused log field; ss -s for connection churn; perf flame graph.
  5. Root cause: each full handshake performs an RSA-2048 signature (~0.7 ms of core), and with 12% reuse almost every connection pays for it. 120k handshakes/s x 0.7 ms = 84 cores for signatures alone.
  6. Fix: ECDSA P-256 certificate (signing is roughly 10x faster than RSA-2048; keep an RSA cert as a fallback for ancient clients); TLS 1.3 only on new clients; session tickets with rotated shared keys across nodes (reuse >70%); enable HTTP keep-alive and HTTP/2 to cut connection count; terminate at a CDN edge near users to cut the 80 ms RTT cost; kernel/NIC accept tuning. Optional: Keyless SSL or HSM offload.
# nginx: shared ticket keys + cache
ssl_session_tickets on;
ssl_session_ticket_key /etc/nginx/tickets/current.key;
ssl_session_cache shared:SSL:50m;
ssl_session_timeout 4h;
  1. Prevention: track handshakes/s and reuse ratio; load test with realistic mixed clients; capacity rule per core.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not 0-RTT for POST; ticket keys need rotation (forward-secrecy exposure window) and secure distribution. Not dropping TLS to save CPU.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Some clients lack ECDSA support? -> Serve dual certs; negotiated per client.
  • Ticket key leaked? -> Recorded sessions that used tickets become decryptable for that window; rotate every few hours.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An edge fleet was sized for RSA signing and scaled linearly with traffic. Switching to ECDSA and fixing a per-node ticket key mismatch (reuse 8% to 74%) cut TLS CPU by two thirds before any new hardware.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: add servers.
  • Hire: ECDSA, resumption and keep-alive.
  • Strong hire: quantifies handshake math, shared ticket keys with rotation, edge termination and fallback certs.
